query: Many physical and chemical fabrication approaches have produced multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles, yet their synthesis–structure–property relationships remain poorly established. This limits evaluation of their suitability for catalytic operation at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric use at 473–1923 K, including catalytic settings where low noble-metal content is desirable. What governs whether these nanoparticles preserve structural and chemical stability under such service regimes, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled intervention that separates it from competing explanations, predict observations relative to a baseline, define its boundary conditions, connect it to the prior evidence summarized above, and provide a clear falsification test.

generation.hypothesis: In HEA nanoparticles used under high‐temperature catalytic or thermoelectric conditions, a high density of defect (or anchoring) sites in the support material reduces the mobility of surface atoms—and in particular, mitigates the evaporation of volatile elements (such as Co or Ni)—by providing energy wells that re‐trap migrating atoms, thereby preserving the nanoparticles’ compositional and structural integrity.
generation.material_initial_state: Multi‐element high‐entropy alloy nanoparticles (e.g., Ru‐5 MEA‐NPs or CoNiCuRuPd) uniformly dispersed on carbon supports.
generation.intervention: Synthesize and deposit identical HEA nanoparticles on two sets of carbon supports: one treated to have a high density of controlled defect sites (via methods such as mild oxidation or plasma treatment) and the other with a low defect density. Then subject both to identical prolonged high‐temperature conditions (773–1173 K for catalysis or 473–1923 K for thermoelectric applications) under controlled atmospheres.
generation.conditions: High‐temperature service conditions (e.g., catalytic operation at 773–1173 K) in an inert or reactant gas atmosphere, with extended exposure times to simulate real operating cycles.
generation.structural_mediator: Defect‐induced anchoring strength at the nanoparticle–support interface, observable as reduced surface atom diffusion and a lower rate of volatile element loss measured by atomic-scale mapping techniques.
generation.mechanism: Defect sites in the carbon support serve as anchoring points that lower the effective diffusion barrier for nanoparticle surface atoms, allowing any atoms that begin to diffuse (or tend to evaporate) to be re‐captured; this effect is especially important for elements with higher vapor pressures under high temperatures. The enhanced local binding reduces net elemental evaporation and delays both phase separation and sintering.
generation.predicted_outcome: HEA nanoparticles on high‐defect supports will display lower rates of compositional drift (i.e., minimal loss of volatile elements such as Co or Ni), improved structural retention (less agglomeration or segregation), and consequently maintain higher catalytic (or thermoelectric) performance over extended high-temperature operation relative to those on low‐defect supports.
generation.baseline: HEA nanoparticles on supports with low defect density or free-standing nanoparticles, which under identical conditions show measurable elemental loss and greater structural changes (e.g., aggregation or segregation).
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to be effective within the thermal regime where atomic diffusion is significant but not so extreme that the support itself degrades. Excessively defective supports or incompatible support chemistries might lead to over-nucleation or other morphological changes that compromise the expected stabilizing effects.
generation.uncertainty: This proposal extends findings from PMC7069714 (which demonstrated that sluggish diffusion from multi-element mixing stabilizes HEA-NPs but noted slight evaporation of Co/Ni at high temperatures) and PMC7733500 (which identified that defects in carbon supports enhance nanoparticle anchoring and thermal stability). The new element is linking engineered support defect density directly to retention of nanoparticle composition under service conditions. Quantitative rates of reattachment and the relevant energy barriers remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of carbon supports with distinctly high and low defect densities (characterized by Raman spectroscopy and surface microscopy). Deposit identical HEA nanoparticles on both support types using the same synthesis protocol. Expose the supported nanoparticles to prolonged high-temperature conditions under controlled atmosphere. Periodically, sample the materials for in situ TEM observation, energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX) mapping to assess elemental composition, and measure catalytic activity (or thermoelectric performance).
measurements: Raman or defect density characterization of supports
In situ TEM imaging for monitoring nanoparticle morphology and potential atom loss
EDX and XPS for compositional analysis (with focus on volatile element retention)
Catalytic or thermoelectric performance tests over time
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no statistically significant difference is observed between the high- and low-defect support samples in terms of nanoparticle compositional stability (e.g., similar loss of volatile elements), structural integrity (similar degree of agglomeration or segregation), and performance retention under identical high-temperature conditions, then the hypothesis—that support defect density directly governs the retention and stability of HEA nanoparticles—is falsified.

The entropy-stabilized structure has less atom diffusion due to high diffusion barriers and sluggish kinetics, resulting in uniform elemental distribution after annealing. Figure 4D shows the statistical probability of the nearest composition distributions for each element in Ru-5 MEA-NPs, displaying its microscopic/atomic arrangement of different elements. We found the nearest-neighbor sites of each element equal to its nominal composition with only short-range fluctuations. As a comparison, when it is fully diffusion equilibrated, clear elemental segregation, especially for Ru, Rh, and Ni, is observed (fig. S5A), indicating that the entropy-induced slow kinetics are the key to stabilize the structure for thermal annealing. cited_evidence.text: The MD simulations indicates that the nanoparticles are quite stable on the edge planes of T-graphite even at extremely high temperatures. To further verify the thermal stability of such nanoparticles, we performed in situ TEM heating on the CNFs decorated with Pt nanoparticles that were synthesized through ex situ Joule heating method. The ex situ formed nanoparticles appear to have very similar morphology to the in situ observations reported in this work. As it can be seen in Fig. 7a, the ultra-fine nanoparticles are located at wrinkled edge planes showing FCC structure (inset of Fig. 7a). The Pt-decorated CNFs are evaluated at various temperatures (573 K, 773 K, 973 K, and 1173 K). As shown in the high angle annular dark field (HAADF)-STEM image in Fig. 7b, the ultra-small Pt nanoparticles are well dispersed on CNF at room temperature (RT). High temperatures are expected to be detrimental to the nanoclusters’ stability, since the nanoparticles would fuse into larger particles to reduce the surface energy at elevated temperatures.
